content.text:
Yes—Needle could be useful, but as an optional first-message hook router, not as the thing deciding whether the learner profile runs.

The learner profile should remain deterministic and mandatory. Needle’s strongest fit is deciding which additional context hooks are relevant to the learner’s first message.

```text
First message
├─ Always: learner profile, session record, active goals
└─ Needle router
   ├─ related topic history
   ├─ due-review context
   ├─ matching long-term goal
   ├─ diagnostic preparation
   └─ no optional context
```

Why it fits: Needle is a tiny, specialized function-calling model rather than a general conversational model. Its architecture is explicitly designed to match queries to tool descriptions, extract arguments, and optionally retrieve top-k tools. That is almost exactly hook routing. It is not intended to replace Keating’s tutor model. [Needle README](https://github.com/cactus-compute/needle), [architecture notes](https://github.com/cactus-compute/needle/blob/main/docs/simple_attention_networks.md).

The best Keating use cases would be:

1. Optional hook selection

Give Needle schemas resembling:

- `load_related_learning_history(topic)`
- `load_due_review(topic)`
- `resume_matching_goal(topic)`
- `prepare_diagnostic(topic)`
- `start_fresh(topic)`

The output becomes a hook decision rather than a user-visible tool call.

2. Topic and intent normalization

For a message such as “I keep getting confused about why promises don’t execute in order,” it could produce:

```json
{
  "topic": "javascript-promises",
  "domain": "computing",
  "intent": "diagnose",
  "hooks": ["load_related_learning_history", "prepare_diagnostic"]
}
```

That could improve artifact metadata, learner-evidence attribution, session grouping, review scheduling, and continuity. Keating should retain the original text and mark the categorization with its source and model version.

3. Lightweight turn classification later

It might eventually recognize signals such as:

- requesting explanation;
- requesting assessment;
- expressing confusion;
- resuming prior work;
- starting a goal.

I would not let that directly change mastery or learner beliefs. It should produce provisional metadata until confirmed by demonstrated performance or explicit feedback.

The main limitation is deployment. Needle currently uses Python 3.11 with JAX/Flax and custom model code, while Keating is a browser PWA. Cactus officially lists React Native and native/server SDKs, but not a web-browser SDK, so this is not presently a drop-in browser model. [Needle package configuration](https://github.com/cactus-compute/needle/blob/main/pyproject.toml), [Cactus SDK matrix](https://docs.cactuscompute.com/v1.14/docs/choose-sdk/). The Hugging Face release is also custom-code BF16 and not served by an inference provider. [Needle on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/Cactus-Compute/needle-hf).

It is also explicitly experimental and requires at least 120 varied examples per tool for fine-tuning; its authors warn that fewer examples overfit and that tiny models can be finicky. [Needle training guidance](https://github.com/cactus-compute/needle#finetuning).

My recommendation would be:

- Keep mandatory hooks deterministic.
- Formalize an optional-hook routing interface now.
- Build an evaluation set from first messages across Keating’s domains.
- Compare Needle against the existing keyword/topic heuristics.
- Initially run it through a local or remote Cactus sidecar behind a feature flag.
- Fail open: timeout or uncertainty simply means no optional hooks.
- Consider browser integration only if Cactus adds a web runtime or Needle receives a practical ONNX/Transformers.js conversion.

So: genuinely promising for hook routing and topic normalization, but I would prototype and evaluate it as a replaceable classifier—not add it to the production browser bundle yet.

You were right: the automatic forks were intended to create same-prompt response pairs for DPO. The missing piece was presentation—the alternative became a confusing child session without asking the learner which answer was better.

That flow now works as an explicit comparison:

- Alternatives remain hidden from the session browser.
- An inline panel shows the alternative with “Keep current,” “Use alternative,” and “Skip” actions.
- Selecting the alternative continues from that response.
- The choice exports as a direct, redacted DPO chosen/rejected pair.
- “Response comparison chance” remains opt-in because every comparison costs a second model request.
